intro:
By the end of this track you can follow one payment from an object on your heap to bytes on a wire, into a database that outlives the code that wrote it, across a call to another service, and through a multi-step process that survives a crash. You will be able to say what each encoding costs in bytes and in risk (lesson 1), change a Protobuf or Avro schema without breaking a reader (lesson 2), run two versions of a service against one database and migrate a live table in phases (lesson 3), call another service with deadlines and retries that can't charge a card twice (lesson 4), and write a Temporal workflow that resumes after a dead worker and a deploy (lesson 5).

The thread through all five lessons is that the writer and the reader of some bytes are never quite the same program: another language, another version, another machine, or the same service a year later. Every lesson starts from something that breaks when you forget that (a rounded ID, a lost field, a double charge, a stuck workflow) and builds up to the rule that prevents it.

You need to read Kotlin and have JDK 21 or newer. The labs live in one Gradle module, `flow`, run from the `labs` folder with `./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.lNN.*'`, and need no code generation: Protobuf is encoded by hand or with `DynamicMessage`, gRPC method descriptors are written in Kotlin, and Temporal runs in its in-memory test server inside the JVM. Only lesson 3 needs Docker, for a PostgreSQL 18 container. The Networking track's lessons on HTTP and on load balancers, timeouts and retries, and the Caching track's lesson on idempotency keys, come up again in lessons 4 and 5.
cheatsheet:
## From objects to bytes (lesson 1)

An object holds addresses that mean nothing outside its process, so data that leaves it is encoded into self-contained bytes.

| Encoding | The sample authorization | Field names in the bytes | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| JSON | 116 bytes | yes | many readers keep numbers as doubles: integers above 2^53 round silently, so send 64-bit IDs as strings; binary data needs Base64 (+33%) |
| MessagePack, CBOR | 84, 85 bytes | yes | smaller values, same names; 39 bytes as a bare array |
| BSON | bigger than JSON | yes | lengths and type bytes, so a database can skip through it |
| Java serialization | | class names | the bytes choose the classes and run their `readObject`: never on untrusted input; JEP 290 filter (`maxdepth=5;com.acme.Order;!*`) |
| Protobuf | 42 bytes | field numbers | never change or reuse a number; `reserved` deleted ones |
| Avro | 38 bytes | nothing | the reader needs the writer's exact schema |

## Schemas that evolve (lessons 2 and 3)

- **Backward** compatible: new code reads old data. **Forward** compatible: old code reads new data. A rolling upgrade needs both, because for a while both versions read and write the same data.
- Protobuf key = `(fieldNumber shl 3) or wireType`. Varints: 7 bits per byte, low bits first; `-1` as `int64` is 10 bytes, as `sint64` 1. Unknown fields are skipped and kept; missing fields read as defaults.
- Avro resolves the writer's schema against the reader's by field name. Add or remove only fields that have defaults.
- Registry modes: BACKWARD (the default) = consumers upgrade first; FORWARD = producers first; FULL = both checks. Non-transitive modes compare only with the latest version: use `_TRANSITIVE` while old data is kept.
- Old code that decodes into its own class and writes the class back deletes fields it doesn't know. Change only what you own, or keep unknown fields.
- Never give an old identifier (a field number, a flag, a column) a new meaning: Knight Capital lost over $460 million in 45 minutes that way.
- Expand and contract: add the new shape, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, drop the old shape after the last old instance is gone. Set `lock_timeout` before DDL on a busy table.

## Calling other services (lesson 4)

| | REST | gRPC |
|---|---|---|
| Contract | OpenAPI 3.2 (YAML or JSON) | `.proto` file, generated stubs |
| On the wire | resource URLs, HTTP methods, JSON | HTTP/2 POST to `/package.Service/Method`; 5-byte prefix + Protobuf per message |
| Outcome | HTTP status | `grpc-status` in trailers (HTTP status is 200) |
| Deadline | none standard; each side sets timeouts | `grpc-timeout`, sent as time remaining and passed to downstream calls (grpc-java, Go) |
| Streaming | no (SSE or WebSocket aside) | unary, server, client, bidirectional |
| Browsers | yes | via gRPC-Web or Connect |

- A remote call can end with no answer, and the client can't tell a lost request from a lost reply. Set a deadline on every call: gRPC has none by default.
- Retry `UNAVAILABLE` and, with a key, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`; never `INVALID_ARGUMENT` or `FAILED_PRECONDITION`. Full-jitter backoff, a cap, one layer. gRPC's own retry policy (service config) retries within the call's original deadline.
- Idempotency key: one per operation, made before the first attempt, sent on every attempt, claimed atomically by the server before the work, passed on downstream. Stripe: up to 255 characters, result saved once execution begins (even a 500), pruned after 24 hours or more, different parameters with the same key are an error, POST only.
- Compatibility: servers deploy first, so requests need backward and responses forward compatibility. Stripe pins each account to a dated version and converts responses back; since `2024-09-30.acacia`, monthly non-breaking releases and two breaking releases a year.
- One gRPC channel = one HTTP/2 connection. An L4 balancer (kube-proxy) pins it to one backend. Fix: L7 per-stream balancing (Envoy, a mesh), client-side `round_robin` over a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`), or `maxConnectionAge` as a stopgap.

## Durable execution (lesson 5)

- Workflow = deterministic code that decides; activity = a step with side effects, at-least-once, retried (Temporal default: from 1 s, doubling to 100 s, no attempt limit).
- The server keeps an append-only event history per run. After a crash, a worker replays the workflow code: recorded steps return their results, the first unrecorded step runs for real. `Workflow.sleep` is a durable timer.
- "Exactly once" = progress recorded once. Pass every external call a key from the workflow ID and step: `"$workflowId/charge"`.
- Saga: each step has a compensation; when a step fails for good, compensate finished steps newest first. No isolation. Put what can't be undone last.
- In workflow code: no `Random`, `UUID.randomUUID()`, clock, `Thread.sleep`, threads or I/O. Use `Workflow.randomUUID()`, `Workflow.currentTimeMillis()`, `Workflow.sleep()` and activities.
- Changing code with runs in flight: `Workflow.getVersion(changeId, Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1)` (old histories get -1), or Worker Versioning to pin runs to their deployment. Replay saved histories with `WorkflowReplayer` in CI. A mismatch raises `NonDeterministicException`, which fails the workflow task and is retried.
- Kotlin 2.4 with Java SDK 1.40: don't pass method references (`activities::charge`) to `Async` or `Saga`; call activities directly or pass a lambda.
- Limits: 51,200 events or 50 MB per history (warnings from 10,240 events or 10 MB); use continue-as-new for long loops.
- Workflow ID as a dedupe key for starts; `REJECT_DUPLICATE` keeps it taken after the run closes.

| Engine (Nov 2026) | Progress recorded in | Resumes by |
|---|---|---|
| Temporal (server 1.32, Java SDK 1.40) | event history in the Temporal cluster | replaying workflow code |
| Restate 1.8 | journal per invocation in the Restate server | replaying the handler |
| DBOS Transact Java 1.2 | checkpoint rows in your PostgreSQL | re-running the workflow with saved step outputs |
| AWS Step Functions Standard | state machine execution history | moving to the next state (exactly-once unless `Retry`) |
| AWS Lambda durable functions | SDK checkpoints | re-running the handler, skipping checkpointed steps |
recap: Data that leaves a process must become self-contained bytes. Java serialization lets the bytes pick classes and run code, so never use it on untrusted input.
JSON is universal but rounds integers above 2^53 in many readers, has no binary type and no schema; binary JSON keeps the field names and saves little.

Protobuf tags each field with a number, so old readers skip unknown fields and missing ones read as defaults; never reuse a number. Avro writes bare values and resolves the writer's schema against the reader's by field name.
Backward compatibility lets new code read old data; forward compatibility lets old code read new data. Rolling upgrades need both, and registries check them before you deploy.
Data outlives code: change a live schema with expand and contract, and never let old code write back fields it doesn't understand.
A remote call can end with no answer. Set a deadline on every call, retry only what didn't get through or is unknown, and only with an idempotency key made once per operation.
REST with OpenAPI and gRPC with Protobuf are two ways to write the contract; gRPC's single long-lived connection needs per-stream or client-side load balancing.
Durable execution records each step's result and replays the code after a crash; activities still run at least once, so every external call carries a key built from the workflow ID.
Workflow code must replay identically: change it with `Workflow.getVersion` or pinned deployments, and test against real histories with `WorkflowReplayer`.

quiz.q: A JavaScript front end reads a payment ID, `1849204436731904017`, from your JSON API with `JSON.parse`. What does it get?
options: The exact ID, because JSON numbers are 64-bit
A parse error, because the number is too large
A rounded number that can match a different payment
The ID as a string, because the parser detects the overflow
quiz.why: `JSON.parse` keeps numbers as IEEE 754 doubles, which hold integers exactly only up to 2^53. Larger IDs round silently to a nearby value. The fix from lesson 1 is to send 64-bit IDs as strings.

quiz.q: Your service reads bytes from a queue with `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` and casts the result to `Order` on the next line. Why is that dangerous if the bytes come from outside?
options: The cast is slow for large objects
The bytes choose which classes are created, and their `readObject` methods run before your cast
Java serialization can't handle nested objects
The cast fails for every class that isn't `Order`, so the service crashes
quiz.why: Deserialization creates whatever classes the bytes name and runs their code first; a gadget chain of ordinary classes on the classpath can end in remote code execution. The `ClassCastException` comes too late. A JEP 290 filter rejects classes before they exist.

quiz.q: A Protobuf field `int64 tip_cents = 7;` was deleted last year. A developer adds `int64 loyalty_points = 7;`. Old records still sit in the database. What happens when new code reads them?
options: Old tips are read as loyalty points, silently
The parser rejects the old records
Field 7 reads as 0, because the old field was deleted
Protobuf detects that the field name changed and skips it
quiz.why: The bytes carry only the field number and wire type, and both match, so the old value lands in the new field. Nothing fails. That is why a deleted number goes into `reserved 7;`, so the compiler refuses to reuse it.

quiz.q: A Kafka topic's Avro subject uses the registry's BACKWARD mode. You register a compatible new schema. In which order do you deploy?
options: Producers first, then consumers
All at once, in one release
It doesn't matter, because the registry converts old data
Consumers first, then producers
quiz.why: BACKWARD means the new schema can read data written with the old one, so the readers (consumers) must have it before any producer starts writing with it. FORWARD is the producers-first mode. The registry checks schemas; it converts nothing.

quiz.q: During a rolling upgrade, v1 and v2 of a service share a table. v2 adds a `loyaltyTier` property to a JSON column. A v1 instance reads such a row into its data class (ignoring unknown properties), changes the amount and writes the class back. What happens?
options: The write fails, because the JSON no longer matches
`loyaltyTier` is deleted from that row
`loyaltyTier` is kept, because JSON columns preserve unknown keys
v1 copies `loyaltyTier` but sets it to null
quiz.why: v1's class has no place for the property, so it never reaches the object, and writing the whole object back drops it. This is the forward-compatibility trap of lesson 3: old code must change only what it owns, or keep the fields it doesn't know.

quiz.q: You must rename the column `email` to `email_address` on a busy table while old code is still running. Which plan never breaks a running version?
options: `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` during a quiet hour
Deploy the new code first, then rename the column
Add `email_address`, write both, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, and drop `email` only after the last old instance is gone
Copy the table, rename the column in the copy and swap the tables
quiz.why: Expand and contract keeps every step compatible with the versions running on both sides of it. A rename breaks whichever version still uses the old name, at any hour. Copying and swapping loses writes made during the copy.

quiz.q: A gRPC client sends 1,000 calls a second through one channel to a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service with 5 pods. Monitoring shows one busy pod and four idle ones. Why?
options: The channel's one HTTP/2 connection was balanced once, at L4, so every call goes to the same pod
gRPC always sends to the first pod in DNS order
The other four pods failed their health checks
Kubernetes balances gRPC per call, but the pods have different CPU limits
quiz.why: kube-proxy picks a pod when a TCP connection opens, and a gRPC channel multiplexes all calls on one long-lived connection. Balance per stream with an L7 proxy or mesh, or in the client with `round_robin` over a headless Service.

quiz.q: Which retry setup can't charge a card twice when replies are lost?
options: Retry `POST /charges` up to 3 times with exponential backoff
Retry with a fresh UUID as the idempotency key on each attempt
Turn on gRPC's retry policy for `UNAVAILABLE`
Make one key per payment before the first attempt, send it on every attempt, and have the server claim it before charging
quiz.why: Only a key that stays the same across attempts lets the server recognize a retry, and claiming it before the work stops two concurrent attempts from both charging. The first three options all resend a request the server can't tell from a new payment.

quiz.q: A Temporal worker dies after an order's `charge` and `reserve` activities completed. Another worker picks the order up. What happens at `charge`?
options: The SDK returns the charge id recorded in the event history; the bank is not called
The SDK calls the bank again, and the key makes it harmless
The new worker skips the workflow code and starts at the next activity
The workflow restarts with a new run ID
quiz.why: Replay runs the workflow code from the top, and every activity call whose completion is in the history returns the recorded result at once. Keys matter for a different moment: an activity that did its side effect but never reported back is run again.

quiz.q: A workflow with 40,000 runs asleep in a 24-hour wait needs a new activity before `charge`. Which deploy is safe for the sleeping runs?
options: Insert the call and deploy; replay skips activities it doesn't recognize
Insert the call behind `Workflow.getVersion`, or pin the old runs to the old deployment with Worker Versioning
Insert the call and restart every sleeping run from the beginning
Rename the activity so the history doesn't match it
quiz.why: Replay must issue the same commands as the history. `getVersion` returns `DEFAULT_VERSION` for histories recorded before the change, so old runs take the old path; Worker Versioning avoids replaying old runs on new code at all. Deploying the change bare raises `NonDeterministicException` and leaves the runs stuck.
